title: A Republican Lawmaker Wants to Make the $100,000 H-1B Fee Permanent Law. Here Is What the PROTECT Act Would Do.
excerpt: Rep. Mike Kennedy filed the bill within 24 hours of a federal judge striking down Trump's executive fee. It would codify the tax at the congressional level — a route that is harder for courts to block.
body:
A federal judge struck down Donald Trump's $100,000 H-1B visa fee on June 8, calling it an unauthorised tax that only Congress could impose. Four days later, Trump's own Justice Department asked the same judge to freeze the ruling. Now a Republican lawmaker has introduced a bill to make the fee permanent anyway — and this time, he wants Congress to be the one doing the taxing.

Rep. Mike Kennedy, a Utah Republican who is also a physician and lawyer, filed the **PROTECT Act** within 24 hours of Judge Leo Sorokin's ruling. The legislation would codify the $100,000 payment at the congressional level, effectively routing around the constitutional objection that sank Trump's executive action.

"The ruling shows we needed somebody in Congress to actually take care of this," Kennedy told the Daily Caller News Foundation.

## What the PROTECT Act Would Do

The bill requires any employer filing a new H-1B petition to pay the greater of the prevailing wage or $100,000 as a base fee. Unlike Trump's proclamation — which applied only to beneficiaries entering from outside the country — the congressional version could be drawn more broadly. Kennedy says the intent is to compel companies to prioritise hiring American-born workers before turning to foreign nationals.

Before Trump's September 2025 proclamation, H-1B filing fees ranged from roughly $2,000 to $5,000 depending on the employer's size. By February 2026, only 85 employers had actually paid the $100,000 fee, according to court filings — a sign of how effectively the cost had frozen demand.

## The Legal Tangle So Far

The H-1B fee has been litigated in at least three federal courts, and the results are a mess. Judge Beryl Howell in Washington, D.C., ruled in the administration's favour in a case brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, finding that Trump's broad immigration powers gave him authority to set the fee. But Judge Sorokin in Boston reached the opposite conclusion a few weeks later, citing the Supreme Court's February ruling that struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs as a precedent for deeming the fee an unconstitutional tax.

A third lawsuit, filed by religious groups and labour organisations in San Francisco, is still pending. The split sets up a likely showdown at the appellate level — possibly reaching the Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, Sorokin himself stayed his own ruling four days after issuing it, meaning the $100,000 fee remains in effect while the government appeals. The stay was widely expected, but it leaves employers in an uncomfortable position: the fee is technically payable, but its legal foundation is crumbling.

## Why This Matters for Indian Workers

Indians receive roughly three-quarters of all H-1B visa approvals. The $100,000 fee has hit Indian IT services firms especially hard — the top Indian employers of H-1B workers saw their approved petitions drop 40 per cent this year. TCS, Infosys, and Wipro have all reported significant declines.

The PROTECT Act would take the fee out of the courts entirely. If Congress passes it, the constitutional question disappears — legislators have the power to levy taxes that presidents do not. For the roughly 300,000 Indians on H-1B visas in the United States, the legislative route is arguably more dangerous than the executive one, because a law is harder to challenge and harder to reverse.

"The substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax, regardless of what the payment is called," Judge Sorokin wrote. The PROTECT Act's answer: fine, we will call it a tax and pass it as one.

## What Happens Next

Kennedy's bill faces long odds in a Congress consumed by other priorities. But the PROTECT Act establishes a template: if the courts keep blocking the fee, sympathetic lawmakers can try to enact it through legislation. The bill also includes provisions requiring employers to demonstrate that no qualified American worker is available before filing an H-1B petition — a requirement that echoes existing Department of Labour rules but could be enforced more strictly.

For NRIs in the United States, the next six months will determine whether the $100,000 fee was a temporary executive experiment or the opening move in a permanent restructuring of the H-1B program. The September expiration date on Trump's original proclamation is approaching. If neither the courts nor Congress settles the question by then, the fee could simply lapse — only to be reimposed under a new proclamation or, if Kennedy has his way, under the force of federal statute.
